chunks: Older and cheaper phones use an ERM, an eccentric rotating mass motor, which is a tiny brushed DC motor, either a coin or a cylinder, with an off-centre weight on the shaft.
When it spins the unbalanced mass shakes the whole phone.
You control it with a DC voltage or PWM, and the stronger vibration comes with higher speed because the force is m e omega squared , so intensity and frequency are tied together.
It's cheap, but it takes tens of milliseconds to spin up and wind down, so the buzz is a bit mushy. Modern phones mostly use LRAs, linear resonant actuators.
That's a voice coil pushing a small mass on a spring along one axis.
You drive it with an AC signal at its resonant frequency, usually around 150 to 250 hertz, so a small drive makes a large motion.
It starts and stops in a few milliseconds, so you get crisp taps and can program waveforms, and amplitude is independent of frequency. You also can't just apply DC to it.
It needs a driver IC that generates the waveform, often with closed loop resonance tracking and active braking.
Piezo actuators are a third option on some devices with very fast response. In short: ERM is simple, LRA is the tight, programmable one."
